etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English today, to-daie, todæig, from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (“today”, literally “on [the/this] day, [this] day forward”), equivalent to to +‎ day. Compare Saterland Frisian däälich (“today”), Dutch vandaag (“today”), Old Saxon hindag (“today”, literally “[this] day forward”), German Low German vandage, vandaag (“today”), Swedish i dag, idag (“today”).

definitions.definition: On the current day or date.
In the current era; nowadays; these days.

quote.citation: 2013 June 22, “Engineers of a different kind”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8841, page 70:
quote.text: Private-equity nabobs bristle at being dubbed mere financiers. […] Much of their pleading is public-relations bluster. Clever financial ploys are what have made billionaires of the industry’s veterans. “Operational improvement” in a portfolio company has often meant little more than promising colossal bonuses to sitting chief executives if they meet ambitious growth targets. That model is still prevalent today.

definitions.definition: (informal) The day of a recurring cycle or event which is currently happening.

quote.text: Yesterday, upon the stair / I met a man who wasn’t there / He wasn’t there again today / I wish, I wish he’d go away …

definitions.definition: (informal or meteorology) From approximately 6am to 6pm on the current day.

quote.citation: 1965, Tom Wolfe, quoting Phil Spector, “The First Tycoon of Teen”, in The Kandy-Kolored Tangerine-Flake Streamline Baby, New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, →ISBN, →OCLC, page 67:
quote.text: Actually, it's more like the blues. It's pop blues. I feel it's very American. It's very today. It's what people respond to today.

quote.citation: 1966 December 18, Joan Barthel, “Francoise from France: White Boots and Ye-Ye”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: […]  she (Françoise Hardy) is so today, so white boots and yé-yé, that she can make anyone over 25 (me) feel prehistoric, raccoon coat and rah-rah.
